must_remember: A symmetric triangular wave has odd symmetry ($x(-t) = -x(t)$), which causes the average value ($a_0$) and all cosine coefficients ($a_n$) to vanish identically.
The Fourier series of a symmetric triangular wave contains exclusively odd harmonics ($n = 1, 3, 5, ...$).
The amplitude of the $n$-th harmonic in a triangular wave decreases quadratically as $1/n^2$, unlike square waves which decay as $1/n$.
The RMS value of a symmetric triangular wave with peak amplitude $A$ is given by $X_{rms} = \frac{A}{\sqrt{3}}$.
Differentiating a symmetric triangular wave with respect to time yields a symmetric square wave.

glossary.meaning: A continuous periodic waveform that alternates linearly between $-A$ and $+A$ with equal rise and fall times.
The set of sinusoidal frequencies present in a complex periodic waveform, which are integer multiples of the fundamental frequency.
The ratio of the peak amplitude to the root-mean-square (RMS) value of a waveform, equal to $\sqrt{3}$ for a triangular wave.
A theorem stating that the total average power of a periodic signal equals the sum of the average powers of its individual harmonic components.
